How old are your youngest? What age do you think it is worth it to start paying for a curriculum?

Our youngest is a year, but the youngest I sit down to try teaching reading/math in a more serious manner is about age 4 to 4.5. Before that it's just reading and counting conversationally. My twins really wanted to do math worksheets like their older sibs, so even though they are 5 and aren't reading yet, they are doing 1st grade math, and I'm reading the sheets to them. I used materials I already owned, though. I've discovered that the reason serious schooling begins in 1st grade around the age of 6, is because kids aren't ready to sit still long enough to learn it before then.

I guess I wouldn't start buying materials until K or 1st grade. I'm also really particular about what we use, and haven't liked free curriculum like "Easy Peasy Homeschool", which is available on the internet. I'm sure it's fine and will get the job done, but it didn't resonate with me. All they need at the beginning is "reading, writing, and 'rithmetic." When they are ready for that, then I would say it's time to buy what you've had your eye on.

The first things I bought were Spell to Write and Read and Saxon Math (whatever was appropriate for the year). SWR is pretty teacher-intensive, but it's been working well for us so far. This has a consumable logbook, but you don't really need it until 1st or 2nd grade, depending on your child's capability, and they are pretty cheap (between $6-$12) You pay around $100 for the core kit, but you use it for about 5 years per child. The only new books you need are the logbook each year. They do also sell enrichment activities books, which I've found helpful.

Saxon 1, 2, & 3 have consumable workbooks, but they are pretty pricey, so what we do is buy them new, tear all the pages out, and put them all in a binder. (Each of my children also has their own school binder for ALL their work.) I'll take the correct lesson worksheets out of my master binder, put them in a plastic page protector, and pop that into my child's binder for that day. They then fill out the worksheet in dry erase marker on the outside of the page protector. There are cons to this method, like they accidentally erase their stuff, or it rubs off with too much movement, but as long as I correct it pretty quickly, then it's not a problem. It's great because I pay once for a set of workbooks, but it'll get used many times.

Doing dishes, making beds, maintaining their rooms, and household chores can all be a part of school. You can think of it as "unit studies" :)

I'm personally in the difficult position of having kids from 6th grade all the way down, so it's hard to balance the various needs of them all. The one thing I do that simplifies things greatly is running a "one-room schoolhouse". Teach multiple children together if possible. The only subjects that I teach individually are Math and English. Everything else is paired with multiple children.

If baby interrupts and you need to nurse or put them to sleep, then it's time for your older children to work on a previously assigned task, household chore, or recess. If you have something to do that you don't want the baby to get into, like a science project, do that when they are napping. If it's a diaper change, include bigger kids. Anyone 8 and older can change a diaper as long as it's not a horrific blowout or other unusual circumstance.

I have also taught my oldest two (ages 11 and 8) to how to cook simple meals. They can make: eggs, ramen, sausage, mac and cheese, chicken&asparagus with rice, PB&J, bake cookies, etc. With my verbal guidance, my 7 year old made a roast with veggies. She did everything. I just put it in the oven.

If you are busy with one lesson, another child can help do meal prep. I teach my kids how to properly use paring knives at age 5 because they are capable of it.
